title.en: Pachacamac, Whom No One Had Seen: Adoration Without Image
title.zh: 無人見過的帕查卡馬克:無像之拜

region.en: Valley of Pachacamac, coast below Lima (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕查卡馬克谷地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The Yncas kings of Peru, with the light of nature which God had bestowed on them, had attained to a conception of the Maker of all things, whom they called Pachacamac, the word signifying the maker and sustainer of the universe. They said that Pachacamac was invisible, and that consequently they neither built temples nor offered sacrifices to him, as to the sun, but adored him inwardly with the greatest veneration, in accordance with the outward demonstrations they made with heads, eyes, arms, and body, when they used his name. Those who had adopted this belief before they were conquered by the Yncas were the ancestors of king Guismancu, who built a temple to Pachacamac and gave the same name to the valley where it stood. The Yuncas placed their idols in this temple, which were figures of fishes, and among them there was the image of a fox. The valley of Rimac, four leagues to the north, took its name from an idol there in the shape of a man, which spoke and gave answers to questions like the oracle of the Delphic Apollo: Rimac signifies 'He who speaks', and the city of Lima was founded in that valley.
summary.zh: 秘魯的印加諸王,憑上帝所賦的自然之光,已能體認造化萬物之主,稱之為「帕查卡馬克」——此名意即「宇宙的造就者與扶持者」。他們說帕查卡馬克隱而無形,故不像對太陽那樣為他建廟獻祭,只在內心以至高崇敬拜他;而每當提及他的名號,便以頭、眼、臂、身作出外在的敬意。此信仰廣布帝國;早在印加人到來之前便已信奉此道的,是庫伊斯曼庫王的先祖——他們為帕查卡馬克建了一座大神廟,並以其名命名所在的河谷。永卡人把偶像供在廟裡:是些魚形神像,其中還有一尊狐像。以北四萊格的利馬谷,則得名於一尊人形神像——它開口言事、有問必答,如德爾斐阿波羅的神諭;「里馬克」即「發言者」之意;今日利馬城便建於該谷。

sensitivity.note: Garcilaso's natural-theology reading of Pachacamac as an unimaged Creator - the classic passage on Andean henotheism.

The Yuncas placed their idols in this temple, which were figures of fishes, and among them there was the image of a fox.

passages.text: The valley of Rimac is four leagues to the north of Pachacamac. The word Rimac is the present participle, and signifies 'He who speaks.' The valley was so called from an idol there, in the shape of a man, which spoke and gave answers to questions, like the oracle of the Delphic Apollo and many others mentioned in the histories of the ancient heathens. So they called it 'He who speaks' because it talked, and the valley was given the same name.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fox, the Ocean, and the Peace with Cuismancu
title.zh: 狐與海:與庫伊斯曼庫的和平之約

region.en: Valleys of Pachacamac and Rimac (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕查卡馬克與里馬克兩谷(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The great lord Cuismancu replied that his people had no need of another lord; that the laws and customs he observed were those which had been received from his ancestors; that his people had no wish to put away their gods, for these gods were very powerful: among them was Pachacamac, whom they believed to be the creator and preserver of the universe, and therefore necessarily a greater god than the sun. They had built a temple to Pachacamac, where they offered up the best of everything they had, even sacrificing men, women and children; and such was the veneration in which they held him that they used not even to look upon his image, but the king and the priests entered the temple to worship, walking backwards, and went out so as to avoid raising their eyes. They also worshipped Rimac, a god that spoke and gave replies; their other objects of worship were the fox, which they respected for his cunning and sagacity, and the ocean, because it supplied them with fish. Cuismancu concluded by saying that these gods were sufficient for them: the sun less than any, as they needed no more heat than they already experienced. The Yncas resolved not to make war but to subdue the Yuncas by reasoning and kindness. A peace was concluded: the Yuncas agreed to worship the sun like the Yncas, and to build a separate temple; that no human sacrifices should be made, because to kill a man was contrary to the laws of nature, and the custom was to be entirely abolished; that the idols should be removed from the temple of Pachacamac, and that he should henceforth be worshipped in the heart, no statue being set up because no one had ever seen him; that a house of chosen virgins of the sun should be established, the two things the provinces most desired to possess being a temple of the sun and a convent of virgins, for by possessing these they resembled Cuzco; and the Yncas agreed to hold in high veneration the oracle Rimac.
summary.zh: 庫伊斯曼庫答道:他的子民不需要別的主;他的法度皆承自祖先;他們也無意拋棄自己的神——那些神威力無邊,其中有創造並扶持宇宙的帕查卡馬克,自然比太陽更偉大。他們為他建廟,獻上最好的所有,甚至人祭;崇敬之至,連神像也不敢仰視——王與祭司入廟禮拜,須倒退而行,出廟時亦不得抬眼。他們還拜里馬克——那尊會說話、有問必答的神;此外尊狐之狡智,敬海洋之賜魚。庫伊斯曼庫說:有這些神便夠了;太陽嘛,他們並不需要更多的熱。印加人聞言大喜,決定不以兵戎,而以理喻與善意收服永卡人。和平條款如下:永卡人奉拜太陽,另建太陽神廟;廢除人祭——殺人違逆自然之法;偶像盡出帕查卡馬克神廟——他既無形無像,自當「心拜」而不立像;並建太陽貞女之屋——各地最慕者,莫過太陽神廟與貞女院,有此二者便如庫斯科;印加人亦允崇奉里馬克神諭,令全境敬之。

sensitivity.note: A negotiated theology: Garcilaso presents the Inca conquest of the coast as a religious peace treaty; the fox-and-ocean cult detail is unique.

passages.text: He replied that his people had no need of another lord... that they had no wish to put away their gods, for these gods, he said, were very powerful. Among them was Pachacamac, whom they believed to be the creator and preserver of the universe, and therefore necessarily a greater god than the sun... such was the veneration in which they held him, that they used not even to look upon his image, but the King and the priests entered the temple to worship, walking backwards, and went out so as to avoid raising their eyes. They also worshipped Rimac, a god that spoke and gave replies to those who sought him. Their other objects of worship were the fox, which they respected for his cunning and sagacity, and the ocean, because it supplied them with fish... the sun less than any, as they needed no more heat than they already experienced.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Yuncas agreed to worship the sun like the Yncas, and to build a separate temple... but that no human sacrifices should be made, because to kill a man was contrary to the laws of nature, and the custom was to be entirely abolished. It was agreed that the idols should be removed from the temple of Pachacamac... Pachacamac was henceforth to be worshipped in the heart, and no statue to him was to be set up; because, as no one had ever seen him, it was impossible to know his figure, or to make an image of him. It was also arranged, for the greater honour and glory of the valley of Pachacamac, that a house of chosen virgins of the sun should be established... The Yncas agreed to hold in high veneration the oracle Rimac.

title.en: The Voice from the Corners of the Temple: Pachacamac's New Oracle
title.zh: 神廟角落的聲音:帕查卡馬克神諭的革新

region.zh: 帕查卡馬克神廟(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: It is worthy of note that the Devil, as soon as he saw that the Yncas had subjugated the valley of Pachacamac, and that the temple was cleared of the numerous idols that it formerly contained, sought to make himself the special lord of it, in the character of the unknown god whom the Indians venerated so highly, so as to obtain worship in various ways, and to sell his lies at a higher price in some places than in others. With this object he began to speak from the corners of the temple to the priests of the highest position and character, saying that he wished to reply to their questions and inquiries, not when all were assembled, but to the most respected alone, because it was beneath his dignity to speak to men of low degree. He added that he could only condescend to converse with kings and great lords, but that he would order the idol Rimac, who was his slave, to speak to the common people, and to answer all their inquiries. From that time it was the rule to consult the oracle on matters of state in the temple of Pachacamac, and for the people to resort to that of Rimac. The latter idol thus had his name of 'Speaker' confirmed, for as he was obliged to answer all, he had to talk a great deal.
summary.zh: 值得注意的是:魔鬼一見印加人征服帕查卡馬克谷、神廟中原有的諸多偶像盡被清除,便趁機自封為此廟特別之主——假冒印第安人至為崇敬的那位「無名之神」,以便受人崇拜、把謊言賣得更貴。為此,他開始從神廟的角落向地位最高、品行最尊的祭司們講話:說他不願當眾作答,只肯對受尊崇者開口——向卑微之人說話有失他的尊嚴;還說他只肯屈尊與君王和大領主交談,至於平民的問詢,則命他的奴僕——里馬克神像——代答。自此以後,國家大事便到帕查卡馬克廟中問神,平民之事則赴里馬克廟求問;「發言者」之名就此坐實——因為他須有問必答,只好喋喋不休。

sensitivity.note: The missionary demonology of oracle differentiation: state cult vs popular cult, narrated in Garcilaso's inherited frame.
